title: Kale microgreen variety selection
subtitle: Which kale varieties work best as microgreens, and how they differ
excerpt: Most kale varieties work as microgreens with minimal difference in the growing process. The main distinctions between varieties are cotyledon colour, flavour intensity, and the speed of the growing cycle. Dwarf Blue Curled, Red Russian, and Black Tuscany (Cavolo Nero) are the most commonly grown.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens variety trials (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Kale microgreen variety comparisons synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: The seed leaf — the first leaf or pair of leaves produced by a germinating seed. In kale microgreens, the cotyledons are harvested as the edible shoot. Different kale varieties produce cotyledons in slightly different colours (blue-green, red-veined, deep green) and with slightly different flavour intensities.

Buying seed specifically for microgreen growing requires checking that the seed is untreated (no fungicide coating). Most standard vegetable kale varieties are available without treatment from garden suppliers and microgreen seed suppliers.

content.text: All kale varieties grow well as microgreens using the same method. The variety changes cotyledon colour and flavour, and sometimes growing speed, but the sowing, blackout, and harvest steps are the same.

are a blue-green to grey-green colour. Dwarf Blue Curled is one of the most widely available kale varieties and produces reliable, even germination. The flavour at the microgreen stage is mild with a slight earthiness. A good first choice.

Red Russian kale produces cotyledons with red-purple veining against a grey-green background. The visual interest at the microgreen stage is higher than most green kale varieties. The flavour is slightly sweeter and less earthy than Dwarf Blue Curled. The seed is slightly smaller and germinates a little faster.

Cavolo Nero produces deep blue-green to nearly black-green cotyledons and a slightly more assertive kale flavour than other varieties. The cotyledons are slightly smaller than Dwarf Blue Curled. Growing time may be a day or two longer. The deep colour makes a striking visual contrast on pale dishes.

Redbor is a curly kale with strong red-purple colour. The cotyledons are red-stemmed with purple-tinged leaves. Growth is slightly slower than other green kale varieties. Redbor gives the most striking colour of all kale microgreens.

: all four varieties are available as untreated vegetable seed from garden suppliers. Microgreen seed suppliers stock them in larger packs (100 g to 500 g) suited to repeated tray growing. For first attempts, a standard 3 g vegetable seed packet produces several 25 cm trays.
